strengths: The paper presents a clear and effective Algorithms/General contribution: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface for VLM-based 3D visual grounding. The design is conceptually simple, well motivated, and addresses a real pain point in transferring 2D VLM reasoning to 3D scenes.

Empirical results are strong on standard benchmarks. The method reports state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance on ScanRefer and Nr3D, with especially convincing gains on relation-heavy/multiple-object settings where panoramic context should matter.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond leaderboard numbers: cross-dataset evaluation on ARKitScenes/SceneVerse and 3RScan/RIORefer, text-variant robustness tests, panorama-vs-pinhole comparisons, modality/objective ablations, camera placement ablations, 3DGS-vs-mesh comparisons, convergence plots, and runtime estimates.

The method is reasonably modular. The panoramic representation, semantic/geometric adapter, visibility-aware lifting/fusion, and EMD coordinate loss are individually understandable and mostly supported by ablations.

The supplementary material improves reproducibility by giving prompt templates, rendering resolutions, LoRA hyperparameters, camera-placement details, two-stage matching details, and auxiliary QA construction.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but not transformative. The main idea combines known ingredients: panoramic rendering, pretrained 2D VLM grounding, adapter-style feature injection, SAM-based masks, and multi-view lifting/fusion. The contribution is more an effective systems/pipeline integration than a fundamentally new grounding formulation.

The approach depends on substantial infrastructure and assumptions: a renderable scene representation, reliable camera poses/trajectories, instance-ID maps during training, precomputed multi-view semantic features, SAM masks, and a 17B VLM fine-tuned with LoRA. This limits practicality compared with lighter 3D grounding models and makes the reported gains partly tied to heavy pretrained components.

Computational cost and reproducibility remain concerns. The paper reports online inference time, but does not fully quantify offline preprocessing time for rendering, feature lifting, semantic-field construction, SAM use, storage, or training cost. For a 17B-backbone method, these details matter for fair comparison and adoption.

Some evaluations change the task setting in ways that complicate interpretation. Cross-dataset and text-robustness experiments use ground-truth object segmentations/candidate instances to isolate language and scene generalization, which is useful diagnostically but does not fully reflect end-to-end 3D box grounding performance.

The ScanRefer evaluation reports only Acc@0.25 in the main comparisons. Reporting Acc@0.5 as well would better show localization precision, especially since the method lifts 2D boxes and masks into 3D and may produce coarse AABBs.

The strongest claims about language reasoning are somewhat indirect. Improved performance on rephrased/affordance/masked queries is promising, but the variants are LLaMA-generated and may contain artifacts or distributional regularities. Human-validated perturbations or error analysis would make the language-generalization claim more convincing.

The paper would benefit from more failure analysis. Limitations mention no-target and multi-target queries, but do not deeply analyze failures from panoramic distortion, occlusion, SAM mask errors, poor reconstructions, tiny objects, repeated instances, or missing semantic features.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving generalization in 3D visual grounding by leveraging stronger 2D VLMs through panoramic renderings. The panoramic interface is intuitive and potentially useful for preserving broad scene context.

The empirical section is broad: ScanRefer, Nr3D/Sr3D, cross-dataset scene transfer, text perturbations, panorama-vs-pinhole comparisons, modality ablations, camera placement ablations, and runtime are all considered.

The reported Nr3D and ScanRefer Acc@0.25 results are competitive, and the cross-dataset/text-variant experiments are a good direction for evaluating robustness beyond standard in-distribution benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely an engineering combination of known components: panoramic rendering, DINO-style semantic features, depth/range features, adapters, SAM lifting, multi-view consistency, LoRA fine-tuning of a large VLM, and EMD-style numeric supervision. The paper does not make a convincing case that the algorithmic novelty is substantial relative to this assembly.

Several claimed gains are modest or mixed. On ScanRefer the main improvement over recent baselines is small, Unique performance is not best, Sr3D is not state of the art, and the ablation table shows geometric features alone slightly hurt performance while the full model improves only marginally over semantic features plus geometric QA.

The evaluation protocols raise concerns. Some generalization and text-robustness results use ground-truth object segmentation/candidate masks, which makes the setting less end-to-end and can substantially simplify the task. The paper should more clearly separate practical deployment performance from oracle-assisted proposal-selection performance.

The method depends on substantial privileged infrastructure: renderable meshes or 3DGS, raw camera trajectories, offline multi-view semantic feature lifting, depth/range rendering, SAM masks, and roughly 9.6 CogVLM-17B forward passes per query. This weakens the practical impact and makes comparisons to lighter 3DVG systems less straightforward.

The state-of-the-art claim is overstated. The paper emphasizes Acc@0.25 but omits common stricter localization metrics such as Acc@0.5 for ScanRefer, and several comparisons are against methods with different inputs, model sizes, or proposal assumptions.

The text generalization benchmark is generated with LLaMA prompts but lacks evidence of human validation, error filtering, or analysis of whether generated affordance/no-name queries preserve the original target unambiguously. The large VLM backbone may also give the proposed method an advantage over baselines not designed for such paraphrases.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important implementation choices for denoising, SAM configuration, aggregation thresholds, adapter insertion details, rendering failures, offline preprocessing cost, and exact training/evaluation variants are either underspecified or scattered into supplementary text.

The limitations discussion is very thin and does not adequately discuss failure cases such as missing/incomplete reconstructions, non-renderable point clouds, small or heavily occluded objects, multiple/no-target queries, dependence on camera trajectories, and computational cost.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and compelling 2D-3D bridge for 3D visual grounding: multi-modal panoramic renderings allow a pretrained 2D VLM to reason over 360-degree scene context while retaining liftable geometry. This is a practical and well-motivated design for the stated Algorithms/General contribution type.

The empirical results are strong. PanoGrounder reports state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance on ScanRefer and Nr3D, with especially notable gains on relation-heavy and human-written language settings. The comparison against pinhole views is convincing and directly supports the central panorama-based design choice.

The paper includes useful ablations: camera placement factors, modality contributions, EMD loss, geometric QA, adapter initialization, number of cameras, test-time rotations, and mesh vs. 3DGS representations. These studies make the technical case substantially stronger than a benchmark-only paper.

Generalization is a major strength. The cross-dataset experiments on ARKitScenes/SceneVerse and 3RScan/RIORefer, plus robustness tests with rephrased, affordance-based, and masked queries, support the claim that the VLM-plus-panorama formulation improves language and scene transfer.

The method is modular and relatively easy to understand: viewpoint selection, panoramic rendering, VLM grounding with lightweight adapters, and visibility-aware 3D aggregation. The supplementary material provides helpful implementation details, prompts, training settings, and runtime measurements.
weaknesses: The comparison to prior 3DVG methods is not entirely apples-to-apples. PanoGrounder uses a large CogVLM-17B backbone, rendered RGB panoramas, multi-view semantic features, depth/range, LoRA fine-tuning, and test-time augmentation, while many baselines operate on different inputs and much smaller architectures. The paper would benefit from a clearer accounting of extra supervision, compute, memory, and pretraining advantages.

The system depends on a renderable scene representation, camera poses/trajectories, and offline panorama/feature preprocessing. This assumption is reasonable for some reconstructed indoor datasets, but it narrows applicability relative to point-cloud-only 3DVG methods and should be emphasized more strongly in the limitations.

Runtime and efficiency remain concerns. Online inference averages 3.30 seconds per query on an A100 and uses about 9.6 VLM forward passes per query due to multiple cameras and yaw rotations. This is acceptable for offline grounding but may limit robotics or interactive use cases unless optimized.

Some generalization evaluations use ground-truth object segmentations or candidate instances to isolate language/scene transfer. This is useful diagnostically, but it weakens the direct evidence for full end-to-end generalization under realistic proposal or segmentation errors.

The method contains several interacting components, and while ablations are good, some design choices remain underexplored: the impact of the specific VLM backbone, the semantic feature source, SAM quality, panorama resolution/aspect ratio, and failure modes for small, occluded, or non-visible targets.

The limitations section is brief and mostly future-looking. It does not fully discuss practical failure cases, dependency on reconstruction quality, fairness of compute-heavy VLM comparisons, or possible deployment constraints.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and technically coherent approach for 3D visual grounding: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface is a simple but effective design that naturally gives VLMs access to wider relational context than pinhole views.

The experimental results are strong. PanoGrounder reports state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer, with especially large gains on human-written Nr3D and multi-object/relational settings.

The paper includes broad evidence beyond the main benchmark table: cross-dataset evaluation on ARKitScenes/SceneVerse and 3RScan/RIORefer, text-robustness tests, zero-shot comparison, modality/objective ablations, panorama-versus-pinhole analysis, camera placement ablations, and runtime/deployment analysis.

The method is relatively modular and practical in spirit: it reuses pretrained VLMs, LoRA/adapters, rendered depth/semantic features, SAM-style masks, and standard reconstruction pipelines rather than requiring a bespoke 3D-language foundation model.

The ablation evidence supports the main design choices. Semantic features, EMD supervision, geometric QA, structured camera placement, and panoramic views each contribute measurable improvements, and the pinhole-view comparison clearly demonstrates the value of the panoramic representation for relational queries.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful figures, implementation details, prompt templates, and supplementary analysis. The limitations section acknowledges important constraints such as reconstruction dependence, speed, and limited target-query settings.
weaknesses: The novelty is more architectural/system-level integration than a fundamentally new learning algorithm. Panoramic rendering, VLM grounding, LoRA/adapters, DINO-style features, EMD digit loss, SAM-based lifting, and cross-view voting are each fairly standard ingredients; the contribution is convincing but somewhat incremental.

The main practical claim is weakened by reliance on renderable 3D scene representations and often clean meshes. The fully automated RGB-to-3DGS setting drops noticeably, excludes ScanNet validation scenes where COLMAP fails, and is evaluated less extensively than the mesh-based setting used for main results.

Efficiency remains a concern. The strongest model uses CogVLM-17B with about 51.6GB GPU memory and roughly 9.6 VLM forward passes per query; the full real-world pipeline also requires substantial offline COLMAP, 3DGS, and semantic feature lifting time and high CPU/GPU memory.

Some evaluations isolate language/scene generalization using ground-truth object segmentations or candidate instances. This is useful diagnostically, but it makes parts of the reported generalization less representative of fully end-to-end 3D grounding under imperfect detection/segmentation.

The ScanRefer improvement over recent single-dataset baselines is modest in the main end-to-end setting, and several gains depend on large pretrained VLM capacity plus test-time rotations. More controlled comparisons at matched backbone, compute, and input assumptions would strengthen the attribution of gains to the proposed panoramic representation.

The text-robustness benchmark is generated by LLaMA prompts and deterministic masking without clear human validation of semantic preservation or ambiguity. Affordance rewrites may introduce dataset/model biases, so the large robustness gains should be interpreted cautiously.

The method is currently limited to indoor/floor-based scenes and axis-aligned boxes, and the authors note it does not handle no-target or multi-target queries. These are reasonable limitations, but they constrain deployment in robotics and open-world vision-language settings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important 3D visual grounding problem and proposes a clear high-level idea: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface so pretrained VLMs can reason over broader scene context than pinhole views.

The manuscript is generally readable and includes substantial experimental coverage: ScanRefer, Nr3D/Sr3D, cross-dataset tests on ARKitScenes/3RScan, text perturbations, ablations, runtime/memory, and a small real-capture deployment example.

The panoramic representation is empirically well motivated. The pinhole-vs-panorama comparison and camera placement ablations support the claim that 360-degree context and viewpoint selection help relation-heavy referring expressions.

The method reports strong numbers on several standard benchmarks, especially Nr3D and ScanRefer Multiple, and the ablations show that semantic features, EMD loss, geometric QA, and camera placement each contribute modestly.
weaknesses: I assess this as an Algorithms/General paper. Under that standard, the algorithmic novelty is limited: the pipeline is largely a composition of existing ingredients, including panoramic rendering, a pretrained VLM with adapters/LoRA, DINO-style feature lifting, SAM-based mask lifting, voting/IoU aggregation, and an EMD auxiliary loss. The paper is more of a systems recipe than a clearly new grounding model.

The main claims about generalizable 3D grounding are weakened by strong input assumptions. The primary results rely on clean renderable scene representations, often mesh renderings, while the fully automated RGB-to-3DGS setting drops notably from about 61.6 to 55.1 Acc@0.25 and excludes scenes where COLMAP fails. This makes the practical robustness claim less convincing than the abstract suggests.

Several evaluations use ground-truth object segments or candidate instances to isolate generalization, including ReferIt3D-style and cross-dataset experiments. This is useful diagnostically, but it also makes the reported generalization less representative of an end-to-end 3DVG system and complicates comparison to methods whose bottleneck includes detection/segmentation.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. The method uses a 17B VLM, large-scale pretrained knowledge, multiple panoramic forward passes with test-time rotations, auxiliary generated QA, and in some cases joint training across datasets. Although the paper groups some training regimes, the compute/model-capacity advantage over many 3D baselines remains a major confounder.

The gains from several claimed technical components are small. The full model improves only marginally over strong internal variants, e.g. semantic+EMD+GeoQA without geometric input is 60.7 versus 61.0 full, and adapter layer placement is essentially insensitive. This weakens the case that the proposed architectural details are central rather than incidental.

The zero-shot comparison is under-specified and potentially misleading. It is unclear how much of the pipeline, feature extraction, prompting, candidate handling, and aggregation differs from prior VLM-grounding methods, and the comparison mixes model families, inputs, and assumptions rather than isolating the effect of panoramas.

The text robustness evaluation is based on LLaMA-generated rewrites rather than human validation. The affordance and noun-masking variants may introduce artifacts or preserve cues in ways that favor VLMs trained on similar language, so the large gains do not fully establish real linguistic robustness.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many implementation details are given, but the pipeline depends on heavy components and choices that can strongly affect results: rendering backend, mesh/3DGS quality, feature lifting, SAM masks, COLMAP failures, VLM fine-tuning, and aggregation heuristics. The paper does not provide enough evidence about variance, failure rates, or sensitivity to these choices.

The practical deployment claim is overstated. The self-captured example contains only one scene and two qualitative queries, while the offline preprocessing cost is large, with high CPU/GPU memory requirements. This is insufficient evidence for broad real-world deployability.

Overall, despite useful empirical observations, the submission does not yet provide a sufficiently convincing scientific case for acceptance: the novelty is modest, the strongest results depend on favorable assumptions, and the comparisons do not cleanly establish that the method’s contributions, rather than scale and preprocessing, drive the reported performance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely Algorithms/General contribution: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface for pretrained VLMs in 3D visual grounding. The representation choice is simple but well motivated, and it directly addresses the field-of-view and context limitations of pinhole-view VLM grounding methods.

The empirical results are strong. PanoGrounder reports state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer, with especially convincing gains on human-written Nr3D and multi-object ScanRefer settings where language and relational reasoning matter.

The paper includes broader evidence than a standard benchmark table: zero-shot comparisons against larger VLM-based systems, cross-dataset generalization to ARKitScenes and 3RScan, robustness to text perturbations, and a self-captured scene deployment. This substantially strengthens the case that the method is not just overfit to one benchmark protocol.

Ablations are thorough and informative. The paper separately studies semantic/geometric features, EMD loss, geometric QA, panorama versus pinhole views, camera placement factors, scene representation, adapter initialization, test-time rotations, and runtime/backbone scaling.

The method is described with enough implementation detail to be largely reproducible, including camera placement, rendering resolutions, prompts, LoRA settings, feature lifting, and the two-stage candidate protocol. The limitations section is also concrete and appropriately scoped.
weaknesses: The practical pipeline is still fairly heavy despite the framing as deployable: the strongest model uses CogVLM-17B with around 51 GB GPU memory and several seconds per query, plus substantial offline costs for reconstruction, semantic feature lifting, and rendering. The smaller backbones reduce cost but also lose much of the headline accuracy.

Some comparisons depend on protocol choices that deserve caution. Generalization experiments use ground-truth object segmentation for all methods, and the ReferIt3D/two-stage variant matches 2D predictions to projected GT instance masks. This isolates language/scene reasoning, but it means those numbers do not fully reflect end-to-end detection/localization difficulty.

The strongest main results rely on mesh-rendered panoramas from clean benchmark reconstructions. The automated 3DGS setting is useful and appreciated, but it is evaluated on a subset where COLMAP succeeds and shows a noticeable drop, so the robustness to raw casual captures is promising rather than fully established.

Several components are inherited or externally dependent, including SAM-style segmentation, DINO-style feature extraction/lifting, 3D reconstruction/rendering, and a large pretrained VLM. The contribution is an effective integration and representation design rather than a fundamentally new model, which is acceptable but limits originality somewhat.

The method is tailored to indoor, floor-based, single-target grounding with axis-aligned boxes. The paper acknowledges limitations around multiple/no-target queries and outdoor/building-scale settings, but these constraints narrow the immediate applicability for embodied agents in less structured environments.
